'''Allan Joseph Champneys Cunningham''' (1842–1928) was a British-Indian [[mathematician]].<ref>A. E. Western, ''J. London Math. Soc.'' 317–318 (1928)</ref>

==Biography==
Born in [[Delhi]], Cunningham was the son of [[Sir Alexander Cunningham]], archaeologist and the founder of the [[Archaeological Survey of India]].<ref name=dnb>{{cite ODNB|author=Cotton, J. S. & James Lunt (reviser)|chapter=Cunningham, Sir Alexander (1814–1893) |title= Oxford Dictionary of National Biography| year=2004| doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/6916}}</ref> He started a military career with the [[British East India Company|East India Company]]'s [[Bengal Engineer Group|Bengal Engineers]] at a young age. From 1871 to 1881, he was instructor in mathematics at Thomason College of Civil Engineering which later became the [[Indian Institute Of Technology Roorkee]] (IIT Roorkee). Upon returning to the [[United Kingdom]] in 1881, he continued teaching at military institutes in [[Chatham, Kent|Chatham]], [[Dublin]] and [[Shorncliffe Army Camp|Shorncliffe]]. He left the army in 1891. He spent the rest of his life studying [[number theory]]. He applied his expertise to finding [[Divisor|factors]] of large numbers of the form ''a<sup>n</sup>''&nbsp;±&nbsp;''b<sup>n</sup>'', such as [[Mersenne numbers]] (<math>2^p-1</math>) and [[Fermat numbers]] (<math>2^{2^n}+1</math>) which have ''b'' = 1. His work is continued in the [[Cunningham project]].
